title: Education
goals: Talk about plans you have already arranged with the present continuous (I'm meeting my teacher on Friday).
Talk about life experiences with the present perfect and ever / never.
Use recently, lately, already and yet to talk about things that have or haven't happened.
Understand and use words about school, college, courses and student services.
Read a report card and talk about grades, attendance and progress.
Take part in a conference with a teacher: ask about progress, ask for help and agree on next steps.
Write a clear, polite email to a teacher.

learn.title: Present continuous for future plans
learn.html:
We use the present continuous (be + verb-ing) for plans that are already arranged. Usually we know the day, the time or the place, and sometimes another person is involved.

FormExample
PositiveI'm meeting my teacher on Friday.
NegativeSheisn't coming to class tomorrow.
QuestionWhat are you doing this weekend?
Short answerYes, I am. / No, we aren't.
  • Use a future time word: tomorrow, tonight, next week, on Monday, this weekend.
  • Use it for arrangements: a meeting, an exam, a trip, an appointment. For a general idea or a prediction, use be going to or will.
  • Verbs like go, come, leave, meet, see and have are very common in this use.

watch.wrong: Tomorrow I'm go to the library.
watch.right: Tomorrow I'm going to the library.
watch.why: After am / is / are, the verb needs -ing.

watch.wrong: What you are doing after class?
watch.right: What are you doing after class?
watch.why: In questions, be goes before the subject.

watch.wrong: I meet my tutor tomorrow at ten. (for a personal plan)
watch.right: I'm meeting my tutor tomorrow at ten.
watch.why: For a personal arrangement, the present continuous is more natural than the simple present.

watch.wrong: We not are having class on Monday.
watch.right: We aren't having class on Monday.
watch.why: The negative is be + not + verb-ing.

learn.title: Present perfect with ever and never
learn.html:
We use the present perfect (have / has + past participle) to talk about life experiences, when we do not say exactly when they happened. Ever means "in your whole life". Never means "not one time in your life".

FormExample
QuestionHave you ever taken an online class?
Short answersYes, I have. / No, I haven't.
PositiveShe has studied in two countries.
With neverI have never failed an exam.
  • Ever goes before the past participle in questions. Never goes between have and the participle. It already has a negative meaning, so do not use not.
  • Some past participles are irregular: take - taken, go - gone / been, do - done, write - written, see - seen.
  • Use been for visits that finished: I have been to the museum. Gone means the person is still there.

watch.wrong: Have you ever went to a science museum?
watch.right: Have you ever been to a science museum?
watch.why: Use the past participle (been / gone), not the past simple (went).

watch.wrong: I never have read a book in English.
watch.right: I have never read a book in English.
watch.why: Never goes after have, before the participle.

watch.wrong: She have never missed a class.
watch.right: She has never missed a class.
watch.why: With he / she / it, use has.

watch.right: I have never studied French. / I haven't studied French.
watch.why: Never is already negative. Do not use a double negative.

learn.title: Present perfect with recently, lately, already and yet
learn.html:
The present perfect also connects the past with now. These words show how the action is related to the present.

WordUseExample
alreadySomething happened before now (sooner than expected)I've already finished my homework.
yetIn questions and negatives; at the end; the action is still expectedHave you registered yet? / I haven't paid yet.
recentlyA short time ago, close to nowThe school has recently opened a new study room.
latelyIn the last days or weeks; at the end of the sentenceI've been very tired lately.
  • Already usually goes between have and the participle, or at the end: I have finished already.
  • Do not use yet in positive sentences. Do not use already in negatives.
  • Recently can go before the participle or at the end. Lately usually goes at the end.

watch.wrong: I haven't finished already my essay.
watch.right: I haven't finished my essay yet.
watch.why: In negatives we use yet, at the end.

watch.right: Have you finished yet? / Have you already finished?
watch.why: Choose one: already or yet. Do not use both.

watch.wrong: She hasn't took the exam yet.
watch.right: She hasn't taken the exam yet.
watch.why: After has / have use the past participle: taken.

watch.wrong: I have yet finished my project.
watch.right: I haven't finished my project yet.
watch.why: Yet goes at the end of negatives and questions.

learn.title: Useful expressions: a conference with a teacher
learn.html:
• Thank you for meeting with me. / Thanks for coming in. — opening the conversation politely.
  • How is my son / daughter doing in your class? — asking about progress.
  • He's doing well, but he hasn't turned in two assignments yet. — giving news with a good point and a concern.
  • Could we talk about his grades? / I'd like to talk about my grade. — introducing a topic.
  • What can I do to improve? / How can we help him at home? — asking for advice.
  • I'm concerned about her attendance. — talking about a worry.
  • Let's make a plan. / Let's meet again in a month. — agreeing on next steps.
  • I really appreciate your help. — closing the conversation.

Dear Mr. Torres,

My name is Laura Mendez, and I am in your English class on Tuesdays and Thursdays. I am writing to ask for a meeting about my grades and my project.

reading.title: Help for Students: Student Services
reading.intro: Read the article about student services at a college and answer.
paragraphs: Starting classes at a college can feel stressful, but most schools have a Student Services Office to help you. This office is usually near the main entrance, and it opens at 8:00 a.m. on weekdays. Many students have never visited it, and that is a mistake.

First, there is the counseling center. A counselor can help you choose your major and plan your courses for each semester. Marta, a new student, has already met her counselor twice. She was not sure about her career, so they looked at her interests and grades together. Now she is planning to study nursing, and she is meeting her counselor again next Tuesday to choose her spring classes.

Second, the tutoring center offers free help in math, writing and English. You can make an appointment online or just walk in. Tutors are usually advanced students who have taken the same course. The library is also part of the service. It has quiet rooms, computers and a printer, and it stays open until 9:00 p.m. during exam weeks. Some students have recently asked for longer hours on weekends, and the school is thinking about it.

Third, the financial aid desk gives information about tuition, payment plans and scholarships. Every year, the college offers about two hundred scholarships, but many students do not apply because they have not read the requirements yet. The deadline for next year is March 15, so it is good to start early. Bring your documents, such as your tax form and your last report card, when you visit.

Finally, remember that these services are free for enrolled students. Carlos, who works at night, says he has been using the online chat lately because he cannot come during the day. He is happy with it. If you have a question and you don't know who to ask, go to Student Services first. Someone there will help you, or they will send you to the right person.

Thank you, Ms. Reyes. I wanted to talk about my grade in biology.
Of course. You have done well on the labs, but you haven't turned in the last essay yet.
I know. I'm finishing it this weekend. Can I give it to you on Monday?
Yes, but only until Monday morning. Have you ever used the writing center at school?
No, I've never been there. Is it free?
Yes, it is. A tutor can read your essay and give you ideas. I'm going there on Wednesday, so I can show you the room.
That would be great. I'm working on Wednesday after school, but I'm free at lunch.
Perfect. Also, you have been late to class three times lately. Is there a problem?
My bus has been late. I'm leaving home earlier next week.
Good idea. Your test scores are excellent, so I want you to keep improving.
